topic: Linear Transformations and Matrices: The Geometry of Change
target_audience: University Undergraduate Students (Introduction to Linear Algebra)

outline.topic: Linear Transformations and Matrices: The Geometry of Change
outline.target_audience: University Undergraduate Students (Introduction to Linear Algebra)

sections.title: The Starting Line: Basis Vectors
sections.content: Introduce the 2D Cartesian plane as a flexible grid. Define the 'basis vectors' i-hat (1,0) and j-hat (0,1). Explain that every vector in the plane is just a combination (scaling) of these two fundamental arrows. This prerequisite knowledge sets the stage for seeing how the entire space moves.
sections.example: Visual: A 2D grid with a red arrow (i-hat) pointing right and a green arrow (j-hat) pointing up. A yellow vector (3,2) is shown as 3 copies of i-hat plus 2 copies of j-hat.

sections.title: Defining Linear Transformation
sections.content: Explain that a 'transformation' is a function that takes an input vector and spits out an output vector. For it to be 'linear', two rules must hold: 1) The origin must remain fixed at (0,0), and 2) All grid lines must remain parallel and evenly spaced. Visually, this looks like the space is being stretched, rotated, or squished, but never curved.
sections.example: Animation: The entire grid morphing—tilting and stretching—while the center point stays perfectly still and the grid lines never bend into curves.

sections.title: The Matrix as a Coordinate Map
sections.content: Reveal the 'Secret': To know where *every* point on the grid goes, you only need to track where i-hat and j-hat land. A 2x2 matrix is simply a shorthand for these two landing spots. The first column is the new coordinate of i-hat, and the second column is the new coordinate of j-hat.
sections.example: Visual: If i-hat moves to (1, -2) and j-hat moves to (3, 0), we write them side-by-side to create the matrix [[1, 3], [-2, 0]].

sections.title: Calculating the New Reality
sections.content: Show the mechanics of matrix-vector multiplication. If we have a vector (x, y), its new position is simply x times the transformed i-hat plus y times the transformed j-hat. This connects the abstract matrix math back to the visual movement of the grid.
sections.example: Formula animation: [Matrix] times [Vector (x,y)] = x * [Col 1] + y * [Col 2]. Watch the vector (2, 3) jump to its new location based on the landing spots of the basis vectors.

sections.title: Application: Transforming 'Leo the Lion'
sections.content: Apply the concepts to a character model. By applying different matrices, we can transform an object in real-time. Show 'Shearing' (sliding the top of the character) and 'Scaling' (making him taller or thinner). This demonstrates how linear transformations are the backbone of computer graphics and character animation.
sections.example: Character: Leo the 2D Lion stands on the grid. Apply a 'Shear Matrix' [[1, 1], [0, 1]]. Leo appears to lean over as if blown by a strong wind, while his feet stay planted at the origin, demonstrating the geometric effect of the transformation matrix.

storyboard.title: The Starting Line: Basis Vectors
lecture_lines: Start with the 2D Cartesian plane's flexible grid.
Meet basis vectors i-hat and j-hat.
Every vector is built from these fundamental arrows.
animations: Create a 2D coordinate grid with color #444444 on a #000000 background.
Animate a red arrow (#FF0000) from (0,0) to (1,0) with label 'i-hat' in white (#FFFFFF).
Animate a green arrow (#00FF00) from (0,0) to (0,1) with label 'j-hat' in white (#FFFFFF).
Introduce a yellow vector (#FFFF00) from (0,0) to (3,2) with label '(3,2)'.
Show the yellow vector as a sum of 3 red 'i-hat' units and 2 green 'j-hat' units.

storyboard.title: Defining Linear Transformation
lecture_lines: A transformation maps input vectors to output vectors.
Linear transformations keep the origin fixed in place.
Grid lines must remain parallel and evenly spaced.
animations: Show the standard grid (#444444) and highlight the origin (0,0) with a white dot (#FFFFFF).
Animate the grid morphing into a skewed shape while the origin stays fixed.
Briefly change grid line colors to cyan (#00FFFF) to show they remain parallel and evenly spaced.

storyboard.title: The Matrix as a Coordinate Map
lecture_lines: Track where basis vectors land after transforming.
A 2x2 matrix records these new landing spots.
Column one is the new coordinate for i-hat.
Column two is the new coordinate for j-hat.
This matrix describes how the entire space moves.
animations: On the transformed grid, show 'i-hat' landing at (1, -2) and 'j-hat' landing at (3, 0).
Display a 2x2 matrix in white (#FFFFFF) with the columns [1, -2] and [3, 0].
Highlight the first column in red (#FF0000) and the second column in green (#00FF00) to match the vectors.

storyboard.title: Calculating the New Reality
lecture_lines: To find a vector's new position, use the matrix.
Scale the new basis vectors by original coordinates.
Add these scaled vectors to reach the destination.
animations: Display the formula 'Matrix * [x; y] = x * Col1 + y * Col2' in white (#FFFFFF).
Animate the vector (2, 3) moving to its new position by scaling the transformed basis vectors.
Highlight the final position of the vector and display its new coordinates in white (#FFFFFF).

storyboard.title: Application: Transforming 'Leo the Lion'
lecture_lines: We can transform complex shapes, like Leo the Lion.
A shear matrix makes Leo lean to the side.
Scaling matrices change his height and width instantly.
animations: Draw a simple 2D lion character outline using gold lines (#FFD700) on the grid.
Transform the lion using a shear matrix [[1, 1], [0, 1]], making it lean right.
Highlight that the lion's base at the origin (0, 0) does not move.
Transform the lion using a scaling matrix [[0.5, 0], [0, 2]] to make it thin and tall.
Animate the lion returning to its original shape through an identity transformation.
